strengths: The paper fills a genuine gap in the literature: while prior work either studied transfer learning in lazy/NTK parameterizations or fixed representations, this is (to my knowledge) the first theory of transfer learning for feature-learning (mean-field/µP) infinite-width networks, covering both Bayesian (replica/Franz-Parisi free energy) and gradient flow (DMFT) settings in a unified framework.

The two main results (adapted feature kernel from a min-max saddle-point problem; stochastic process equations for two-stage gradient flow with elastic weight coupling) are technically substantive and derived carefully in extensive appendices, including explicit closed forms for linear networks, train-test kernels, and a CNN extension.

The theory is validated quantitatively: the analytical predictions match finite-width (N=20000) Langevin/gradient-descent simulations remarkably well across linear, polynomial (low-to-high and high-to-low degree Hermite teachers), and real (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST) settings.

The phenomenology is interesting and actionable: the interplay between elastic coupling δ, feature learning strength γ0, dataset size P2, and task similarity (e.g., transfer helps when the source is richer; transfer from high- to low-degree tasks can hurt unless γ0 is large; transfer benefits concentrate in the small-target-data regime) provides interpretable insights that go beyond the trivial 'similarity helps' statement.

The writing is generally clear, the related-work section is thorough and positions the contribution against [40,41], [14], [26], and deep linear model work [42] honestly, and limitations (two-layer networks, no dataset averaging) are candidly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental relative to the building blocks: the Bayesian machinery is a direct adaptation of the aNBK replica framework of [14], and the DMFT extension follows [26], with the transfer learning twist (elastic coupling) borrowed from [40,41]. The main new content is combining these ingredients under µP scaling and adding the elastic penalty, which reduces the conceptual novelty.

Scope is narrow: two-layer networks only, square loss/regression and two-class classification, grayscale downsampled 28x28 images. Real-data experiments are small-scale (P1, P2 in the hundreds), so the claim that the theory 'applies to real datasets' is demonstrated only in a weak regime far from modern transfer learning practice.

The replica-symmetric ansatz is assumed without justification ('the only solution that makes sense' is asserted, page 17); no check of RSB stability or discussion of when RS might fail, which is a standard concern for Franz-Parisi potentials in high-dimensional landscapes.

The theory tracks P×P kernel matrices without averaging over data, so the saddle-point equations become unwieldy for large datasets — a practical limitation that limits applicability and is only mentioned as future work.

Several results are intuitively foreseeable (more task similarity → more transfer benefit; source richer than target helps; warm starts from overly complex features hurt), so the headline qualitative findings, while nicely quantified, may not surprise experts in transfer learning theory.

Some presentation issues: a dangling reference 'Eq. ?', the incomplete condition in Eq. (58) (C.5.4 states the setup 'in principle, in this case,' with no matrix given), occasional typos ('A a detailed derivation', 'do not recover', 'when γs = γs'), and Figures 7/8-9/12 appear only in the appendix while important for the conclusions.

Missing comparisons with simpler alternative baselines (e.g., kernel regression on the frozen source kernel, linear probing vs full fine-tuning beyond the limiting cases) that would strengthen the practical significance of the adaptive-kernel theory.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question — a predictive theory of transfer learning in feature-learning regimes — and combines two complementary formalisms (Bayesian/replica analysis via a Franz-Parisi potential, and DMFT for gradient flow with weight decay) in a single framework for two-layer mean-field/µP networks.

The derivation of the adapted feature kernel via saddle point equations, and the identification of the elastic weight coupling δ as the parameter controlling feature reuse, is a coherent and technically non-trivial contribution; limiting cases (lazy limit, δ→0, δ→∞) are correctly recovered and interpreted.

Theory–experiment agreement is reasonably convincing: the saddle-point and DMFT predictions track Langevin/gradient dynamics on N=20000 networks across linear, polynomial (staircase-style), and image datasets (CIFAR-10, MNIST/Fashion-MNIST), including non-trivial phenomena such as negative transfer from high- to low-degree teachers.

The phenomenology extracted (interplay of task similarity, feature learning strength γ0, dataset size P2, and elastic coupling) is interpretable and connects to related literature (kernel-task alignment, grokking, fine-tuning/linear probing).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the two core results are essentially direct extensions of existing machinery — the Bayesian analysis closely follows Lauditi et al. [14] with an added elastic penalty (itself borrowed from Ingrosso et al. [40] and Shan et al. [41]), and the DMFT result extends Bordelon & Pehlevan [26]. The main genuinely new ingredient is the elastic coupling δ, whose conceptual contribution is modest.

The replica-symmetric ansatz is adopted with essentially no justification ('staring at these equations the only solution that makes sense...'); no replica-symmetry-breaking analysis, instability check, or discussion of when RS may fail is provided, leaving a central technical assumption unverified.

Scope is narrow: theory and experiments are limited to two-layer networks; the real-data experiments are small-scale (CIFAR-10 downsampled to 28×28 grayscale, P2 ≤ 200, two classes), so the claimed relevance to practical transfer learning / fine-tuning is weakly supported. The connection to fine-tuning (Sec. 4) is only a qualitative remark.

Several clarity and presentation problems: broken cross-references ('From Eq. ?'), typos ('A a detailed derivation', Figure 10 caption 'When γs = γs'), inconsistent notation (δ vs η used interchangeably for the elastic coupling, e.g., Eqs. (36) vs (58)), and Figures 1–13 with small, hard-to-read panels. Eq. (58) also appears inconsistent with Eq. (37) in the power of the kernel inside Φ̂.

The evaluation lacks ablations a reviewer would want: no systematic comparison against simpler baselines (e.g., NNGP/NTP transfer baselines from [40, 41]), limited error bars or averaging over seeds/datasets in the real-data experiments, and no quantified measure of theory-experiment deviation; claims that theory 'accurately predicts' generalization are mostly supported visually.

The elastic penalty on first-layer weights only is a modeling simplification that is not standard in transfer learning practice; the paper does not clearly justify this choice or test sensitivity to where the penalty is applied.

Significance is limited by the known narrow-regime validity: results hold at P = ΘN(1) with fixed data, and the authors themselves note the theory does not average over datasets, which restricts how general the insights are beyond toy settings.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: no prior theory of transfer learning exists for feature-learning (mean-field/µP) nonlinear networks, especially validated on real datasets; prior work either assumed fixed representations or relied on Gaussian-equivalence/NNGP limits where transfer vanishes.

Provides two complementary theoretical frameworks — a Bayesian replica/Franz-Parisi free energy (Result 1) and a DMFT analysis of two-stage gradient flow with weight decay and elastic coupling (Result 2) — showing transfer learning produces adaptive kernel predictors whose kernels depend on both source and target data/labels.

The elastic weight coupling δ and feature-learning strengths {γ̄0, γ0} give interpretable knobs, and the phenomenology is convincing: transfer helps most when tasks are aligned, larger δ helps when the source is richer than the target, and warm-starting can hurt when transferring high-degree to low-degree polynomial features unless target richness is large.

Substantial and generally convincing theory–experiment agreement: Langevin simulations match the Bayesian saddle-point equations, gradient descent matches DMFT on N=20000 networks for linear, polynomial/Hermite, and real image tasks, including learned kernel structure (Figs. 1-2, 9) and preactivation distributions (Figs. 6, 11).

Appendices are detailed and self-contained: full replica derivation, test-point coupling for generalization error, closed-form linear-network solutions for several special cases, CNN extension, and an honest positioning against prior work [40, 41, 14] explaining where the new theory differs (non-Gaussian preactivations, adapting kernels, non-vanishing transfer at α→0).
weaknesses: Scope is limited to two-layer networks; real-data experiments use small 2-layer MLPs (and a 2-layer CNN) on grayscale downsampled CIFAR/MNIST/Fashion-MNIST with tiny sample sizes (P2 = 50-200), so the claim of relevance to modern transfer learning/fine-tuning practice is largely aspirational.

The methodological novelty is moderate: the elastic-coupling Franz-Parisi setup is borrowed from [40, 41], the Bayesian formalism extends [14], and the DMFT analysis extends [26]. The contribution is a combination/adaptation of existing machinery to the transfer setting rather than new technical tools; no head-to-head empirical comparison against the competing theories of [40, 41] is provided to substantiate the claimed superiority.

The theory does not average over datasets, so saddle-point equations scale with the number of datapoints; consequently there are no scaling-law predictions, and practical applicability is limited to small P.
Replica-symmetry ansatz is assumed without justification ('the only solution that makes sense'), and no replica-symmetry-breaking stability analysis is offered.

Presentation is not fully polished: a broken cross-reference ('From Eq. ? we get' in Appendix C.5.1), inconsistent notation (η vs δ in C.5.1/C.5.4), figure caption typos (Fig. 1 lists '(c)/(d) γs ≤ γt' twice; Fig. 10 says 'γs = γs'), and grammatical errors ('A a detailed derivation', 'This adaptations', 'Firstly derived') suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.
The connection to fine-tuning (lazy target + large δ ≈ linear probe) is stated only qualitatively; low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and layer-preservation questions are deferred to future work.
Some empirical observations (e.g., the grokking-like overfit-then-adapt behavior in Fig. 5) are conjectural and not rigorously connected to the theory.

strengths: Substantive theoretical contribution: extends mean-field/DMFT analysis of infinite-width feature learning to the two-stage transfer learning setting, covering both fine-tuning (lazy downstream) and jointly rich (feature learning on both tasks) regimes, which prior kernel-theory works (Bordelon et al., Canatar et al.) could not address.

Derives interpretable closed-form results: explicit test-loss formulas in the proportional limit for data-rich pretraining (Result 2), finite-source-data noise/crosstalk decomposition of the adaptive kernel into signal spike, noise spike, and crosstalk terms (Result 3), and an ultra-rich collapse result (Result 4), yielding a coherent phase diagram of positive/negative transfer.

Connects theory to practice across a hierarchy of experiments: linear toy models, polynomial tasks (easy→hard vs hard→easy transfer), and real datasets (CIFAR-10, MNIST/Fashion-MNIST), with DMFT simulations matching finite-width gradient descent reasonably well.

Comprehensive and mostly self-contained appendices (DMFT primer, path-integral derivations, Bayesian/Franz-Parisi extension), which supports reproducibility and positions the work carefully against concurrent Bayesian transfer-learning theories (Ingrosso et al., Shan et al., Aminian et al.).
weaknesses: Real-data experiments are phenomenological and small-scale: two-layer ReLU MLPs on class-pair regression subsets of CIFAR-10 do not strongly test the generality of the theory to modern deep architectures; the claimed transfer to real settings is qualitative rather than quantitative.

Some derivations are not fully closed: the finite-data kernel structure in Appendix C.2 is an ansatz, and the constants c1, c2, c3 are left as undetermined functions of (γ1, ν1); the connection to real datasets requires an additional ansatz (Fig. 2a), weakening the strength of the quantitative predictions.

Result 2 partially recapitulates known spiked-kernel results from Bordelon & Pehlevan (2022); the truly novel content is in the finite-data and ultra-rich regimes, which could be more clearly foregrounded.

Presentation issues: inconsistent notation (γ0 vs γ1 in Fig. 2 caption and Appendix C), typos ('which might can be higher', 'theory from 1'), and dense derivation-heavy exposition that makes the main-text claims harder to follow.

Assumptions (isotropic Gaussian data, linear/rank-structured tasks, two-layer networks for the analytic results) limit the scope of quantitative predictions; the paper acknowledges this but the gap between theory and modern practice remains sizable.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and under-theorized question: when and why transfer learning succeeds or fails, using an infinite-width feature-learning (mean-field/µP) framework rather than the lazy NTK limit, which allows representation adaptation during both pretraining and downstream training.

The overall technical machinery is substantial: a general two-stage DMFT formulation for arbitrary depth (Appendix B), a Markovian specialization to two-layer networks (Result 1), average-case generalization analyses of linear toy models in the proportional limit (Results 2-4), and a Bayesian/replica extension via a Franz-Parisi free energy (Appendix F) that is carefully positioned against Ingrosso et al. (2025) and Shan et al. (2025).

The phase-diagram conclusions are interpretable and well organized: data-rich pretraining always helps fine-tuning (Result 2), finite source data induces noise/crosstalk spikes that can cause negative transfer (Result 3), and ultra-rich pretraining collapses features to a rank-one spike so that only aligned targets are learnable (Result 4). These qualitative regimes are plausible and consistent across linear, polynomial, and CIFAR experiments.

The linear toy model yields closed-form test losses (Eqs. 8, 13, 15) with clear limiting-case analyses (Appendix C), and the appendix derivations (path-integral DMFT, saddle-point equations, DMFT Monte-Carlo solver details) are generally self-contained and reproducible in spirit.

The experimental validation strategy is sensible: DMFT predictions are compared against finite-width gradient descent on polynomial and CIFAR-10 tasks, and the qualitative phenomena (optimal feature-learning strength, negative transfer with data-poor sources, diminishing transfer benefit as P2 grows) show up consistently.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core framework: the main theoretical engine (two-layer mean-field DMFT, adaptive kernel at convergence, kernel regression readout) is essentially the framework of Bordelon & Pehlevan (2022) and Lauditi et al. (2025) applied sequentially to two tasks. The genuinely new analytic content is thin: Result 2's kernel and loss follow nearly directly from prior work, and the Bayesian appendix largely re-derives Lauditi et al. (2025) with an elastic coupling already introduced by Ingrosso et al. (2025).

The most novel claim (Result 3, the finite-data adaptive kernel with signal, noise, and crosstalk components) rests on an ansatz for the limiting kernel structure (Eq. 120). The authors admit that computing the constants c1, c2, c3 'is in principle hard' and leave them as undetermined functions; conclusions about negative transfer are then drawn only for special alignment cases (αs = 1, αg = 0) and via additional ansätze (e.g., Fig. 2(a) sets c_i = functions of χ by analogy with Result 4). This weakens the rigor of the paper's central quantitative claims.

Several rigorous-looking statements are loose: Result 3 states the downstream loss 'might can be higher than the baseline' without characterizing when; Result 4's 'ultra-rich' regime is obtained via a balanced-initialization limiting argument whose connection to actual gradient flow at large finite γ1 is only asserted; the claim that deep networks' adaptive kernels 'have the same functional form' is a belief, not a result.

The experimental evaluation is narrow: real-data validation is limited to CIFAR-10 regression on two-class pairs with a two-layer ReLU MLP (P2 = 200-1000), a setting far from where transfer learning matters in practice (deep architectures, classification, large-scale pretraining). No experiments test the phase boundaries quantitatively (e.g., measured c1, c2, c3 from trained kernels against theory); comparisons are phenomenological rather than predictive.

The practical significance of the findings is questionable: conclusions such as 'transfer helps when tasks are aligned and the source has enough data' and 'too much feature learning can hurt' are largely expected from prior intuition and from empirical transfer-learning literature; the theory rarely delivers a prediction that could not have been anticipated, and the phase structure is only established in isotropic-Gaussian linear models, which the authors themselves acknowledge limits quantitative relevance.

Presentation issues reduce readability: Results 2-4 are dense and depend heavily on appendix material; notation is inconsistent across sections (γ0 vs γ1, ν vs η for the elastic coupling, Eq. 246 'but that in principle, in this case,' is an incomplete sentence); several equations in the appendices have typos or unexplained steps (e.g., Eq. 128's '1/D νX2D'); the abstract's claim of 'interpretable conclusions' oversells what are mostly qualitative trends.

The DMFT solver is validated only visually against finite-width runs at N = 20000, with no error bars, no study of N-scaling of the agreement, and no discussion of finite-width corrections, even though finite-width effects (e.g., noise spikes at finite ν1) are central to the story.

strengths: The paper develops a genuinely new theory of transfer learning in infinite-width feature-learning (mean-field/μP) networks, covering both fine-tuning (lazy target training on adaptive source kernels) and a jointly rich regime where feature learning occurs on both source and target tasks — a setting not covered by prior kernel-based transfer theories (Canatar et al., Tahir et al., Ingrosso et al.) or by Bayesian NTK-proportional analyses.

The linear toy-model analysis is a clear highlight: closed-form test losses in the population regime (Result 2), finite-sample effects producing a noise spike, crosstalk and signal decomposition of the adaptive kernel (Result 3), and an ultra-rich limit showing rank-one feature collapse (Result 4). Together these give an interpretable phase diagram of when transfer helps vs. hurts (negative transfer, optimal feature-learning strength, ridge-like regularization from uncorrelated noise), which goes qualitatively beyond existing transfer-learning theory.

The two-stage DMFT result (Result 1) for two-layer networks is technically substantive, making history dependence from pretraining explicit and Markovian in the two-layer case, with an honest discussion of why deeper models break this structure (Appendix B).

The theory is validated at multiple levels: single-site Monte Carlo DMFT simulations against finite-width gradient descent on polynomial tasks and CIFAR-10 (Figs. 3, 4), and phenomenological agreement of predicted trends (optimal γ1 vs P2, advantage shrinking with target data) on real data (Fig. 2). The Bayesian Franz-Parisi extension (Appendices E–F) adds breadth and clearly distinguishes the contribution from Ingrosso et al. (2025) and Shan et al. (2025).
The paper is well-positioned in the literature and transparent about limitations (isotropic data, two-layer focus, ansatz-based kernel constants) in the discussion.
weaknesses: Some central results rest on assumptions/ansätze rather than complete derivations. In particular, the finite-data kernel structure of Result 3 (Eq. 11/120) is assumed ('Ansatz on the kernel structure'), and the coefficients c1, c2, c3 are explicitly left unsolved ('Computing the constants ... is in principle hard. We leave them as constants'). Consequently the headline phase-diagram claims about negative transfer depend on postulated scalings of these constants (e.g., the ansatz used in Fig. 2a and Fig. 8), weakening the quantitative force of the theory.

Experimental validation is narrow. Real-data experiments are limited to CIFAR-10 regression on two classes with a two-layer ReLU MLP (width 20000), small P2, and kernel regression rather than end-to-end fine-tuning on the downstream task. There is a substantial gap between the regimes where the theory is exact (infinite width, isotropic Gaussian data, population/proportional limits) and where it is merely checked phenomenologically.

The technical novelty is largely a transfer-learning extension of the existing DMFT machinery of Bordelon & Pehlevan (2022, 2023) and Lauditi et al. (2025); the path-integral derivations in Appendices A–C follow known templates, and several results (e.g., the population-limit spiked kernel, χ = sqrt(1+γ²)−1) are explicitly attributed to prior work.

Notation and presentation issues reduce clarity: inconsistent symbols between main text and appendix (γ1 vs γ0 for source richness), a sign inconsistency in χ (sqrt(1−γ₁²)−1 in Fig. 2 caption vs sqrt(1+γ₀²)−1 in Appendix C.1), typos ('which might can be higher', 'niose'), and Eq. 203 appearing to give an expression inconsistent with Eq. 15 in the main text (ν1 vs 1 normalization), which reviewers would need to check carefully.

Key insights (alignment controls transfer; too much feature learning can hurt; finite source data induces noise) are intuitive and partially anticipated by prior empirical/linear-theory work (Tahir et al., 2024; Graldi et al., 2024; Aminian et al., 2024); the added value is quantification in the mean-field limit rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the DMFT Monte Carlo solver and Langevin-sampling experiments are described at a high level, but no code release is mentioned, and reproducing the many-parameter figures (with the unsolved c-constants) would be difficult.
